identification.bodyShape: Elongated, laterally compressed mackerel body with a deeply forked tail and a lateral line that slopes gradually from the gill cover to the tail rather than dipping sharply.
identificationTraits: Sides carry numerous irregular golden-yellow to bronze spots with no connecting streaks or lines.
Front of the first dorsal fin is marked with a bluish-black blotch — the clearest single field mark separating it from king mackerel, which lacks this blotch.
Lateral line slopes gradually to the tail, unlike king mackerel's abrupt downward dip under the second dorsal fin.
identification.coloration: Bluish-green to olive back, silvery sides and belly, sides marked with scattered gold-to-bronze spots.
identification.adultAppearance: A slim, silver-sided mackerel with a black-blotched front dorsal fin and scattered gold spotting, lacking the horizontal yellow streaks of cero mackerel.

similarSpecies.name: King mackerel (Scomberomorus cavalla)
similarSpecies.distinction: King mackerel lack the black dorsal-fin blotch and gold spotting typical of adult Spanish mackerel, run considerably larger, and show an abrupt downward dip in the lateral line under the second dorsal fin.

similarSpecies.name: Cero mackerel (Scomberomorus regalis)
similarSpecies.distinction: Cero mackerel show a horizontal row of yellow-orange streaks along the midline mixed with spots above and below, rather than the spots-only, no-streaks pattern of Spanish mackerel.

identification.averageAdultLength: Commonly around 15 in as landed; adults reach at least about 28 in (70 cm) fork length.
identification.commonAnglingSize: Roughly 14-20 in and 1-3 lb in the recreational fishery.
identification.typicalWeight: Often under 3 lb; Florida's rod-and-reel record is about 12 lb.
identification.maximumDocumentedSize: Up to about 36 in and 13 lb; South Carolina's state record is 11.0 lb (1983).
identification.longevity: Males live to about 6 years; females to about 11 years.

gaps: A single continent-wide average adult length figure; regional/latitudinal variation was not fully resolved.
External sexual dimorphism beyond differing growth rates and maximum age was not found in reviewed sources.

social.note: Forms schools that move and feed together, cooperatively packing small baitfish into tight bundles before striking; not a lie-holding solitary predator.

feedingStrategy.note: Coordinated schooling attack that bunches small schooling fish (anchovies, menhaden, herring, small jacks) before striking; opportunistic on shrimp and squid when present. Diet capacity is not evidence of a current bait event.

dielTendency.note: Reviewed agency sources document a strong temperature-driven seasonal presence pattern but do not establish a sourced day/night feeding preference; recorded as a gap rather than assumed.

behavior.thermalDrivenBehavior: Presence tracks water temperature closely. Historical accounts place a preferred band near 70-80°F, while fishery-independent survey data from 1990-2013 show regular occurrence up to about 86°F and a marked drop-off in occurrence below about 65°F. Fish largely leave an area once nearshore/bottom temperature falls under roughly 70°F heading into fall.
behavior.currentFacing: Concentrates where tide-driven current compresses baitfish against a beach cut, jetty, inlet mouth, or reef edge rather than holding a current break as a resting lie.
behavior.depthMovement: Stays high in the water column; occurs over reefs and grass beds as well as open water with no bottom structure at all.
behavior.coverUse: Uses reefs, jetties, and artificial reefs opportunistically as places bait concentrates, not as cover in the way a structure-oriented ambush predator would.
behavior.spawningBehavior: Multiple-batch spawner on the open coastal shelf from April into late September, timing shifting with latitude. A single large female can release 500,000 to 1.5 million eggs over a season. Spawning water and any staging concentration are conservation context only and are not described as holding water.

diet.primaryNote: A piscivorous coastal pelagic; primary prey is small schooling baitfish (anchovies, menhaden, herring, shad, small jacks, pompano, mullet, needlefish), supplemented by penaeid shrimp and squid. Diet capacity is not evidence of a current bait event.

lifeStageDiet.youngOfYear: Larvae feed on the larvae of other open-water schooling fishes.
lifeStageDiet.juvenile: Smaller individuals feed heavily on anchovies.
lifeStageDiet.adult: Larger fish remain fish-dominated in diet but take proportionally fewer anchovies and more of other baitfish species, plus shrimp and squid.

diet.preySizeShifts: Prey composition shifts from anchovy-dominated toward a broader mix of baitfish species and crustaceans/squid as fish grow.
diet.observedForageRule: Diet capacity is not proof that a bait event is happening now; observed current forage still comes from a direct sighting, not from this dossier.

seasonal_calendar.overview: Spanish mackerel presence is driven almost entirely by water temperature: winter concentration off Florida and in the western Gulf, a spring push north along the Atlantic coast and into surf, pier, and nearshore water, summer occupation of surf/inshore/nearshore water through much of the range, and a fall retreat south as water cools below roughly 70°F. Spring-through-late-summer spawning is conservation context, not a fishing cue.

entries.habitatClass: Concentrated in Florida and western Gulf nearshore/coastal waters as more northern waters fall out of the active thermal band.
entries.thermalContext: Largely absent from water under about 65°F.
invalidators: Expecting Spanish mackerel presence in cold, off-season water north of Florida or the western Gulf overwintering grounds.

entries.habitatClass: Moves onto beaches, piers, jetties, and nearshore reefs as coastal water warms through the 70-80°F preferred band; reaches North Carolina by around April.
entries.forageEmphasis: Schools of small_forage_fish pushed onto beaches, jetties, and nearshore structure.
entries.presentationImplication: Run-and-gun cast and surf metal cast / surf swim retrieve to visible schools working bait in the surf and along structure.
entries.conservationNote: Spawning begins in April; spawning water is conservation context only.
invalidators: Fishing far offshore for a species that is running the beach and nearshore structure this season.

entries.habitatClass: Occupies surf, inshore grass-flat/channel-edge water, and nearshore reefs and piers through peak thermal season (mid-Atlantic occurrence by June).
entries.thermalContext: Within or above the 70-80°F preferred band; survey data show continued occurrence up to about 86°F.
entries.presentationImplication: Live-bait slow troll and horizontal retrieve over nearshore structure; run-and-gun casting to visible surface schools inshore and in the surf.
entries.conservationNote: Peak spawning season; spawning water is excluded from holding-water guidance.
invalidators: Treating a single hot spell as a bite-timing signal rather than a seasonal presence pattern.

entries.habitatClass: Southward coastal retreat toward Florida and the western Gulf as water cools; still available along piers, jetties, and nearshore structure ahead of the full seasonal withdrawal.
entries.presentationImplication: Surf metal cast and run-and-gun cast remain effective as schools move through on the retreat.
invalidators: Expecting the same nearshore/surf availability once bottom temperature drops under roughly 70°F.
